newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine, Romania, Moldova agree to cooperate.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine, Romania, Moldova agree to cooperate.

text.p: Romania and the former Soviet republics of Ukraine and Moldova agreed to form a free economic zone on Thursday and U.S. Vice President Albert Gore praised them for boosting European security.

Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma and Emil Constantinescu of Romania -- which is seeking quick entry to NATO alliance -- said the summit had been made possible by a treaty signed last month burying disputes over borders and minorities.

"There is a huge will in Ukraine, Romania and Moldova to cooperate on a trilateral basis. It's something new which the world will appreciate because this area, not so long ago, was considered a zone of potential conflicts," Constantinescu told a news conference.
"Our cooperation is the best recognition of the priority of European values."
Kuchma said Gore had called him in the Danube river port where the three countries virtually touch to congratulate the leaders on their contribution to European security.
Romania is seeking early entry to NATO at next week's Madrid summit despite the U.S. preference to limit initial expansion to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Conclusion of a treaty with Ukraine was widely seen as a key condition for boosting Romania's chances.
The free economic zone covers the Danube delta area between the ports of Reni in Ukraine, Galati in Romania and Giurgiulesti in Moldova.

"Foreign capital and private investment never goes to unstable regions," Kuchma said. "We opened new prospects and the first step is a free economic zone. This will give the people of three countries a chance to live better."

Moldova and Romania, linked by strong ethnic and cultural links and common use of the Romanian language, enjoy close links though calls for reunification after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union have largely died down.
"We want to live in peace and cooperation and we are oriented towards the future -- despite having very many difficult events in the past," said Moldovan President Petru Lucinschi.
All three countries have had to cope with political turmoil in the post-communist era.
Hundreds of people died in 1992 in fighting between Moldovan troops and Slav separatists in its Dnestr region.
Romania dealt with outbreaks of ethnic and political unrest in the immediate aftermath of the violent 1989 overthrow and execution of Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Ukraine has been spared violence but has had to extend broad autonomy to its Crimean peninsula to meet the demands of pro-Russian separatists.
